response.answer: For mixed clinical data, use Target Encoding for high-cardinality categorical features and Normalizing Flows for continuous data. Fallback to frequency binning for implausible encodings.

results.content: # Dealing with categorical features with high cardinality: Target Encoding. *One very common step in any feature engineering task is converting categorical features into numerical.* Categorical data can pose a serious problem if they have high cardinality i.e too many unique values. What is the most suitable way of including categorical variables that have a very large number of unique classes? * **Label Encoding** (scikit-learn): i.e. mapping integers to classes. While it returns a nice single encoded feature column, it imposes a false sense of ordinal relationship (e.g. 135 > 72). * **One Hot / Dummy Encoding** (scikit-learn): i.e. expanding the categorical feature into lots of dummy columns taking values in {0,1}. This is infeasible for categorical features having e.g. I understand that models will struggle with sparse and large data. This article will talk about **target encoding or *mean encoding.***. In Mean Encoding we take the number of labels into account along with the target variable to encode the labels into machine comprehensible values. ## Written by Kumar Vishwesh. ## Responses (1).

results.content: * **Design** effective preprocessing pipelines for datasets with high-cardinality categorical features using advanced methods like Target Encoding and understand the risks of data leakage. * **Optimize** feature engineering workflows by selecting the most appropriate encoding scheme based on the nature of the data, the chosen machine learning model, and production constraints. This chapter delves into the theory and practice of categorical data encoding, a crucial step in the feature engineering pipeline that directly impacts the performance, interpretability, and efficiency of machine learning systems. We will explore Target Encoding, a powerful yet delicate technique that leverages the target variable to create rich, informative features, while carefully navigating its primary pitfall: data leakage. Target Encoding, also known as Mean Encoding, is a powerful technique for handling high-cardinality nominal features. A category that appears only once will be perfectly encoded with its own target value, creating an artificially perfect predictor that will not generalize to new data. > **Tip:** Target encoding is highly effective for tree-based models like Gradient Boosting and Random Forests, which can effectively handle continuous features and capture the complex relationships it creates. Let’s now tackle the high-cardinality `product_id` feature using Target Encoding. The plot clearly shows that the target-encoded feature effectively captures the predictive signal from the `product_id` category. Higher encoded values correspond to higher target values, creating a powerful continuous feature for a model to learn from. By encoding the category with its historical fraud rate (the mean of a binary ‘is\_fraud’ target), the model gains a powerful feature indicating the baseline risk associated with that type of merchant, without creating thousands of new columns. * **Implementation:** High-cardinality features like `product_id` or `user_id` are often encoded using embedding techniques. They can handle ordinally encoded nominal data better than linear models because they partition the data based on thresholds (e.g., `city_code < 3`). * **Advanced Strategies:** To handle high-cardinality features, we explored **Target Encoding**, a powerful method that uses the target variable to create a dense, predictive feature. * **One-Hot Encoding (OHE):** A process of converting a categorical variable into a set of binary features (0s and 1s), where each new feature represents a unique category.

results.content: # Encoding of categorical variables with high cardinality. * **One Hot / Dummy Encoding** (scikit-learn): i.e. expanding the categorical feature into lots of dummy columns taking values in {0,1}. That is not to say you cannot utilise them in encoding other categorical features. This might help Quantile Encoder: Tackling High Cardinality Categorical Features in Regression Problems:. > The most well-known encoding for categorical features with low cardinality is One Hot Encoding [1]. However, when dealing with high cardinality categorical features, one hot encoding suffers from several shortcomings [20]: (a) the dimension of the input space increases with the cardinality of the encoded variable, (b) the created features are sparse - in many cases, most of the encoded vectors hardly appear in the data -, and (c) One Hot Encoding does not handle new and unseen categories. > An alternative encoding technique is Label/Ordinal Encoding [3] which uses a single column of integers to represent the different categorical values. In target encoding, categorical features are replaced with the mean target value of each respective category. This Medium article I wrote might help as well: 4 ways to encode categorical features with high cardinality. It explores four encoding methods applied to a dataset with 26 categorical features with cardinalities up to 40k (includes code):. * CONS: risk of target leakage (target leakage means using some information from target to predict the target itself); when categories have few samples, the target encoder would replace them by values very close to the target which makes the model prone to overfitting the training set; does not accept new values in testing set. * PROS: limited increase of feature space (as compared to one hot encoding); does not grow in size and accepts new values during inference as it does not maintain a dictionary of observed categories; captures interactions between features when feature hashing is applied on all categorical features combined to create a single hash. * PROS: limited increase of feature space (as compared to one hot encoding); accepts new values during inference; captures interactions between features and learns the similarities between categories. 1") Encode categorical variables with many labels.
